For once the occasion is barely disputed. Adam Clarke reports that the Hebrew and all the versions give the psalm to David and that four of them state it was composed on the rebellion of his son, adding that nothing in the psalm positively disagrees with that inscription. John Calvin notes the same addition in some copies and says interpreters generally agree it is the most probable occasion. Keil and Delitzsch observe that some codices of the old Greek carry no inscription at all while others carry that one, and read the psalm as coming out of the situation of a king persecuted by his son; they add a distinction between the two groups of persecution psalms, that in these later ones the mourning of a dethroned king is deepened into melancholy by blending with the penitential sorrow of a man conscious of his own guilt, which is why the church chose this for the last of its seven penitential psalms. Augustine of Hippo accepts the title and passes through it, since all those past events were figures of things to come and we must recognise here another David, strong in hand, which is what the name means.

Which righteousness is being appealed to occupies them all. Matthew Henry has the psalmist explain rather than correct his own plea: he means the righteous promises of the gospel and not the righteous threatenings of the law, since if he were answered according to the righteousness of the broken covenant of innocency he would be quite undone. John Calvin guards the word the same way, denying that it speaks of merit or hire, as some ignorantly imagine, and making it the goodness of God which leads him to defend his people, the best proof of his faithfulness being that he does not forsake those he has promised to help. Augustine of Hippo makes it a commendation of grace, so that none of us think his righteousness his own,. Charles Ellicott divides the pair, the first word recalling the covenant promise and the second the conviction that the Judge of all the earth must do right. Adam Clarke reads the following petition as a plea against the court itself: do not come in either as a witness against me or as a judge, else I am ruined.

How the same prayer can invoke justice and then shrink from it is noticed by two of them. Charles Ellicott observes that the divine justice has just been invoked and that the appellant now suddenly seems to deprecate it, and finds in these verses the very paradox of the book of Job, where the sufferer pours out protestations of innocence in one breath and in the next dreads that God should take him at his word and arraign him; man appeals to the just Judge in his desire to be vindicated before men, and instantly falls back with a guilty sense that before that tribunal none can stand. He adds that the clause about being justified follows the old Greek and would better be rendered that none living is just. C.H. Spurgeon describes the same movement as a change of court: the psalmist was somewhat inclined to lay his case before the bench of justice, but prefers to turn it all into a petition and present it elsewhere, and so cries hear my prayer rather than hear my suit, being specially earnest that his own life should not become the subject of a trial. John Gill reaches the same conclusion by inventory, since neither his nature nor his heart nor his thoughts nor his words nor his actions would bear examining. Adam Clarke follows the darkness of the third verse into the caves and dens of the earth and even the tombs, and Charles Ellicott renders the desolate heart of the fourth more literally as one that fills itself with astonishment.

That the second half is built out of older psalms is noticed by both critics, who then part company over what follows from it. Keil and Delitzsch say the psalm here seems still more like a reproduction of the thoughts of earlier psalms, tracing the cry for a speedy answer, the plea that God not hide his face, the expression of languishing longing and the closing clause about those who go down into the pit each to its model. Charles Ellicott allows the dependence and denies the inference: it does not detract from the reality of the feeling expressed by means of these ancient sobs and cries, and the contrast of the present with the former times just recalled makes the anguish the more intense, the longing the more consuming and the supplication the more urgent. Matthew Henry reads the same urgency off the opening word, since the psalmist begins not only as one in earnest but as one in haste, though the haste is not of unbelief but of vehement desire; and he adds that those who through grace are delivered from going down to the pit may still, when the terrors of the Almighty array themselves against them, look like men who are going to it. C.H. Spurgeon answers in kind, that mercy has wings to its heels when misery is in extremity.

What the morning means is settled in four ways. Adam Clarke takes it as a matter of fact: the petition was probably offered in the night, when messengers had been despatched in all directions, and the prayer is that some good news might come by daybreak. John Gill agrees that it was then night and reports two Jewish readings which make the morning the springing out of a redemption and the time of salvation, a season of distress being called the evening. Charles Ellicott allows either the plain sense of early or a figure for the dawn of hope. John Wesley reduces the word to seasonably and speedily. C.H. Spurgeon keeps it in the ear rather than the eye: sorrow has made the man deaf, and there is but one voice that can cheer him, which he would hear at the first dawning hour.

The petition for guidance is taken as literally by one as it is spiritually by the rest. Adam Clarke reads it as a request for directions on the road, since the rebels were in possession of all the country and the fugitive did not know which way to go without falling in with them, so that he asks providence to point out the path. Charles Ellicott makes it the way at once of duty and of safety, and John Gill the practice of God’s revealed will and submission to it under affliction. On the next clause Charles Ellicott would not read that the spirit is good but rather that the good spirit may lead him, and renders the promised country a level land, taken metaphorically of tranquillity; Adam Clarke keeps it as the place where he shall be safe, and gives his old Psalter, that the good Spirit shall lead him into the right land. Charles Ellicott also renders the clause about fleeing to God literally, that unto thee have I hidden, allowing the sense that he confided his troubles there but preferring the reflexive, that he fled and hid himself. John Gill closes on the paradox of the last verse, that what is an act of vindictive justice to the enemies is an act of grace to the man delivered from them, and Adam Clarke that they would, if they succeeded, destroy the very form of godliness.
